newsitem.title: USA: Simpson offers no explanation for blood, cuts on hand.
newsitem.headline: Simpson offers no explanation for blood, cuts on hand.

text.p: O.J. Simpson testified on Monday he could not explain the blood found inside his Ford Bronco and at his estate or account for some of the cuts on his hand following the murders of his ex-wife and her friend.

During Simpson's second day on the witness stand in his civil trial, Daniel Petrocelli, lead attorney for the plaintiffs, mounted a scathing attack on the former football star's alibi for the night Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman were killed. He also accused him of failing a lie detector test.

Simpson testified mostly in a calm, confident voice, but when asked about a phone call in which police informed him of his ex-wife's death, he squirmed uncomfortably, sighed heavily and spoke at times with a tremor in his voice.
Petrocelli confronted Simpson in dramatic fashion about blood found dripped in his Bronco, inside his mansion and on the driveway of his multimillion-dollar estate.

The attorney contended some of the unexplained injuries to Simpson's fingers and hand were caused by fingernails "ripping into your skin," suggesting it happened in the death struggle between Simpson and his alleged victims.
Simpson was acquitted of the double-murder in October 1995, but is now facing a wrongful death civil suit brought by the victims' families.

Simpson said he recalled seeing only one speck of blood on the little finger of his left hand just before he went to the airport for a flight to Chicago on the night of June 12, 1994, but could not remember how he sustained the injury.
"You don't have any explanation for blood matching your blood and DNA ... in that Bronco, do you?" Petrocelli asked.
"That's correct," Simpson said.
"You don't have any explanation of how the blood of Nicole was found on that carpet (in the Bronco)," Petrocelli insisted.
"No," Simpson replied.
Simpson's attorneys are expected to mount a defence based on a theory that blood at the murder scene and at Simpson's estate was planted by police in a conspiracy to frame him.
Simpson said he suffered a gash to the middle finger of his left hand when he broke a drinking glass in the bathroom of his Chicago hotel room after being told of his ex-wife's death.

Petrocelli showed Simpson and the jury photos of several other cuts and abrasions on his left hand. Simpson denied the cuts were there when he returned from Chicago, but admitted he had no explanation for how he received them.

Simpson also denied taking and failing a lie-detector test two days after the murders. In an answer to Petrocelli, he said he went a private polygraph expert for a demonstration of how a lie detector test worked, but as far as he was concerned it was only a demonstration.

"And you did take the test and you failed, true?" Petrocelli asked. "That's not correct," Simpson answered. "You got a minus 22, one of the lowest..." Petreocelli said before being cut off by Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki.
Simpson agreed with Petrocelli that he had been "wired up" but said, "I didn't exactly take a lie detector test. I wanted to know what the process was."
"Minus 22 is a score indicating extreme deception, right?" Petrocelli asked before the judge again cut him off.

Petrocelli also attacked Simpson's alibi that he was home at the time of the murders, arguing he had changed his story about vital evidence in the case. Petrocelli said Simpson told police in an interview conducted the day after the murders that he had been driving in his Bronco and made a call on his cellular phone to his girlfriend, model Paula Barbieri.

Simpson's cellular phone records showed the only call made that night was at 10:03 p.m., putting Simpson in the Bronco at that time, Petrocelli said. The plaintiffs' attorneys contend the killings occurred around 10:35 or 10:40 p.m.
Simpson told police his last action before leaving for the airport was to take his cellular phone out of the Bronco. But on Monday he testified he had taken it out hours earlier.
"You don't want it to be in the Bronco at 11 p.m. If it's there at 10 p.m., then you weren't at home at 10 p.m. and that would destroy your alibi, wouldn't it," Petrocelli said.

But Simpson maintained the transcript of the police interview was incomplete, that he told police he had taken his cellular phone accessories -- a carrying case, spare battery and an adaptor -- out of the Bronco at the last minute.
Simpson told the jury that around the time of the murders he was variouly chipping golf balls in the dark, taking a shower and sitting on his bed reading.
